title: CHAPMAN v. THE UNITED KINGDOM
summary:
In Chapman v. the United Kingdom, the applicant, Ms. Jane Chapman, is a British citizen who identifies as a Gypsy by birth, falling within the Council of Europe’s definition of Roma and Travellers. The case highlights the vulnerability of Roma and Traveller communities who, due to a shortage of authorised sites and restrictive planning laws, are often unable to pursue their traditional way of life without facing legal penalties. Ms. Chapman and her family, lifelong travellers in Hertfordshire, purchased land in 1985 to settle in a caravan after years of being moved on by authorities and experiencing harassment that disrupted their children’s education and family health. Despite repeated applications, local authorities consistently refused her planning permission to live on her own land, citing Green Belt restrictions, and issued enforcement notices that led to fines and forced the family back into a precarious nomadic existence.

The European Court of Human Rights examined the case under Articles 6 (right to a fair hearing), 8 (right to respect for private and family life), 14 (prohibition of discrimination), and Article 1 of Protocol No. 1 (protection of property). The case was declared admissible, meaning the Court found the complaints raised serious questions under the Convention, but at this stage, no violation was found or remedies awarded.

Chapman v. the United Kingdom is significant as it addresses the persistent barriers Roma and Traveller families face in securing stable accommodation and exercising their cultural rights, reflecting a broader historical context of marginalisation and exclusion from mainstream housing policies in Europe.
